sections.heading: Coming to you through Jesus
sections.text: Father of mercy, please hear me because I belong to Jesus, not because I have earned your attention. Even when I am trying to walk closely with you, sin is still mixed into me. If you had dealt with me as I deserved, I would not be here now. But you have been patient and kind. You gave me faith in Christ and his cross. Through him you brought me back to yourself, and you brought my heart back toward you. In myself I am guilty, but in Christ you count me clean and accepted.
theological_themes: God receives sinners through Jesus Christ, not through personal merit.
The cross reconciles guilty people to God.
Justification means being counted righteous in Christ while having no righteousness of one’s own.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes reconciliation as God’s own work through Christ, climaxing in the exchange by which sinners are counted righteous in him. This grounds the prayer’s confidence that acceptance with God rests on Christ, not on the believer’s performance.

This passage connects Christ’s death for the ungodly with justification, reconciliation, and salvation from God’s judgment. It supports the prayer’s honest confession of guilt alongside confidence in mercy through the cross.

sections.heading: Asking for grace to live what I believe
sections.text: You are the giver of every grace I have. Please keep strengthening what you have begun in me. I know the truth, but I find it hard to live it. I believe your promises, yet I still need your power to obey them. Help my faith become practical in the choices I make today.
theological_themes: All spiritual growth is a gift of God’s grace.
Believers are called to live out what they believe, while depending on God to work in them.
Faith is not merely agreement with truth but trust that bears fruit in obedience.

scripture_references.connection: Paul holds together the believer’s active obedience and God’s active work within them. This fits the prayer’s request for strength to practice what is believed.

Peter teaches that God supplies what is needed for life and godliness, and that believers are to grow in the qualities that flow from faith. This supports asking God to preserve and increase his graces in the believer.

sections.heading: Owning my weakness and deep sin
sections.text: Please strengthen me against temptation. My heart is not a small problem I can manage on my own. Sin keeps finding ways to flow out of me, and it has been there longer than I like to admit. You have stripped away the things I used to rely on, and I can see more clearly now that I have no real strength apart from you. You alone can restrain what is evil in me. If your grace does not hold me up, I fall.
theological_themes: Human sin is deep, persistent, and not curable by self-reliance.
God’s grace both exposes false confidence and becomes the believer’s only strength.
Dependence on Christ is necessary for obedience and perseverance.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that fruitful life is possible only by abiding in him, and that apart from him his disciples can do nothing. This directly supports the prayer’s confession of helplessness without God’s sustaining grace.

David’s confession treats sin as something deeper than isolated actions and asks God for inward cleansing and renewal. This illuminates the prayer’s unsparing view of the heart and its need for God’s intervention.

sections.heading: Needing protection in the fight
sections.text: When temptation comes, I can be set on fire so quickly. The faith that should protect me can feel weak in my hands. I am not clever enough or strong enough to outlast the enemy by myself. Protect me from Satan’s schemes and attacks. Keep me awake to my danger, but not despairing. Keep me aware of my weakness, and even more aware that your strength is enough.
theological_themes: Temptation involves real spiritual conflict, not merely internal struggle.
Faith must be actively exercised, yet believers need God’s power to stand.
Knowing one’s weakness is meant to drive dependence on God, not despair.

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers to stand against the devil’s schemes in the strength of the Lord, including taking up the shield of faith against flaming darts. This is the biblical background for the prayer’s language about Satan’s attacks and God-given protection.
Paul warns against self-confidence in temptation while also promising God’s faithfulness and provision. This supports the prayer’s balance of sober weakness and trust in sustaining grace.

sections.heading: Let trials teach me to depend on you
sections.text: Father, let every trial teach me more of your peace and more of your love. Do not let hard things make me colder toward you. Use them to draw me nearer. You have given me your Holy Spirit to grow your grace in me, and I cannot keep or deepen that grace unless he keeps working in me. By your Spirit, steady my trust in your promised help. Teach me to walk humbly, leaning on you for everything, because of Jesus.
theological_themes: God can use trials to deepen endurance, hope, peace, and knowledge of his love.
The Holy Spirit sustains and increases grace in the believer.
Christian perseverance is humble dependence on God’s promised help.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that suffering can produce endurance, character, and hope because God’s love is poured into believers’ hearts through the Holy Spirit. This strongly supports the request that trials would teach more of God’s peace and love.
The fruit of the Spirit describes the character God produces in those who live by the Spirit. This supports the prayer’s dependence on the Spirit to preserve and increase grace in daily life.
James presents trials as a means by which God matures steadfast faith. This helps ground the prayer’s request that trials would not be wasted but would lead to deeper dependence and growth.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s statement that God has 'reconciled thyself to me and me to thee' could be read in more than one way. I preserved the biblical substance of reconciliation through Christ without implying that God was morally changed or corrected; the emphasis is on God’s gracious action to restore guilty sinners to himself.

The original uses very strong language about indwelling sin from childhood. I kept that force because it reflects classic doctrines of original sin and remaining sin in believers, though some Christian traditions would express this with different nuance.
The prayer’s direct reference to Satan’s attacks reflects a biblical spiritual-warfare framework. I retained it without adding speculative details about demonic activity.
significant_interpretive_choices: I understood 'it is of thy mercy I died not long ago' as a confession that only God’s mercy has preserved the sinner from deserved judgment and kept him alive for repentance, rather than as a reference to a specific illness or near-death event.
I rendered 'graces' as the Spirit-given qualities and strengths God plants in a believer—faith, obedience, humility, perseverance—rather than as separate sacramental acts or generalized blessings.

I kept the movement of the original: appeal through Jesus, confession of sin and justification in Christ, request for strength to live out faith, confession of weakness in temptation, resistance to Satan, and dependence on the Spirit through trials.
